title: Welcome
body: Runes are letters and symbols. We'll learn them by sound, shape, and meaning — then reinforce with short reviews.

title: The Aetts
body: An aett is a grouping of eight runes; the twenty-four Elder Futhark runes divide into three. The groupings and their conventional names are traditional. Freyr's Aett (also called Freyja's) covers creation and wealth — physical life, primal energy, growth, and material or personal wealth. Hagal's Aett, also named for Heimdall, covers change and trial — forces outside our control, tests, trials, and deep personal transformation. Tyr's Aett covers order and spirit — human nature, society, justice, breakthrough, the divine, and achievements of the mind. Treat those thematic readings as a modern teaching frame rather than an attested historical claim, and use the grouping as a pacing tool: learn a small batch, then review before moving on.

title: Gods: Aesir & Vanir
body: In Norse tradition, the divine community is often described with groups such as the Aesir and the Vanir. Aesir are commonly framed as the gods of sovereignty and war, while Vanir are linked with fertility, prosperity, and well-being. In practice, you’ll see rune correspondences and lore reference both groups.

title: Functions: Sovereignty / Strength / Production
body: A helpful high-level lens is a three-function model: sovereignty (rulership/sacred authority), strength (war/protection), and production (fertility/wealth). When you learn a rune, try to notice which function its themes lean toward — it improves recall.

title: Runic Correspondences
body: Some systems attach correspondences (trees, herbs, beings, colors, tarot, astrology). Treat these as optional mnemonics: useful for memory and ritual structure, not strict dogma. This app includes a compact correspondence set so you can explore patterns and build your own notes.

title: Practice
body: Short sessions, frequent review. Accuracy first, speed later. Grade honestly; the scheduler works best when you do.

title: Yggdrasil
body: Many rune traditions use the World Tree as a memory-map: roots, trunk, and branches correspond to layers of experience. Use it as a mental scaffold for placing gods, worlds, and runes into a single picture.

citations.note: Public-domain translation used for cosmology framing.

title: The Nine Worlds
body: The worlds framework (Asgard, Midgard, Hel, etc.) is a narrative tool. In the app, treat it like a graph: nodes are worlds, edges are travel/relations, and lore entries link to the nodes.

title: Origin of Runes
body: Common stories connect rune-knowledge with sacrifice, ordeal, and disciplined practice. The takeaway for learning: slow, deliberate repetition beats binge-studying.

title: Seiðr
body: Seiðr is often described as a form of Norse magical practice. In this curriculum we treat it as historical/cultural context plus a memory aid for correspondences, not as a promise of outcomes.

title: Odin and the Rune-Ordeal
body: A common teaching story ties rune-knowledge to Odin's self-sacrifice and sustained ordeal. Use the myth as a learning rule: train like a craft — deliberate reps, clear notes, and honest review.

title: Tyr, Oaths, and Tiwaz
body: Tyr is often framed around duty, law, and keeping one's word — even when it costs. When studying Tiwaz, practice a simple oath: pick one tiny habit (5 minutes a day) and keep it for 9 days.

citations.note: Tyr and the binding of Fenrir.

title: Thor, Boundaries, and Thurisaz
body: Thor stories are often used to model protection and strong boundaries. Thurisaz is frequently taught with the idea of 'threshold force' — power at the gate. In study: ask, 'what am I protecting, and what should I keep out?'

title: Freyja and Seidr
body: Freyja is commonly associated with seidr in later lore discussions. For this app, treat it as context + mnemonic: combine a water-themed rune (Laguz) with a growth-themed rune (Berkanan) to remember 'flow + cultivation'.

title: Freyr, Prosperity, and Ingwaz
body: Freyr themes often include prosperity, peace, and the 'right season' for growth. Ingwaz is commonly taught as contained potential that ripens into release. Pair it with Fehu to remember: resources → stewardship → harvest.

title: Rune Poems: A Memorization Map
body: The rune poems are short verses that pair each rune-name with a vivid image or proverb-like line. For study, treat them as a mnemonic layer: name -> image -> meaning -> sound -> shape. We use the poems as a cross-check, not as a single authoritative meaning.

citations.note: Public-domain translation hosting Anglo-Saxon and Norwegian rune poems.

title: Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem: Kennings and Images
body: The Anglo-Saxon poem is useful even if you focus on Elder Futhark: it preserves a pattern of “name + teaching image.” When you see a rune, ask: what is the concrete thing (cattle, aurochs, thorn), what is the social meaning (wealth, strength, protection), and what is the behavioral advice (share, endure, respect)?

title: Norwegian Rune Poem: Compressed Associations
body: The Norwegian poem is short and often cryptic. Use it as a “signal,” not a full explanation: if a rune is consistently linked to a specific natural force, tool, or social obligation, that is a strong hint about its core association.

title: Völuspá: Mythic Timeline and World Order
body: Völuspá is a “big picture” spine: creation, the ordering of beings, the fate-thread, and the catastrophe/renewal cycle. When adding lore, you can tag entries by where they fit in the arc: creation, ordering, conflict, doom, renewal.

citations.note: Public-domain translation used for the mythic arc.

title: Ragnarok: Doom and Renewal (Not Just “The End”)
body: Ragnarok is described as catastrophe and renewal. For study, treat it as a cycle: signs, collapse, confrontation, aftermath, and re-emergence. This helps you connect lore entries to a consistent structure rather than isolated facts.

title: Mead of Poetry: Inspiration as a Substance
body: In the Eddic tradition, “poetry” is not only skill — it is a mythic substance that can be gained, guarded, stolen, and distributed. For the app, you can tag inspiration entries (speech, song, learning, creative fire) and connect them to Ansuz/Kenaz study and Odin as a patron of insight.

citations.note: Public-domain translation used for motif framing.

title: Norns, Fate, and Wyrd: How “Destiny” Works Here
body: The Norns are often treated as a system: past, present, and future constraints weaving together. For study, treat fate as “constraints + consequences,” not passive inevitability. This makes rune work and journaling prompts more grounded: what constraints exist, what actions fit the path, what are the consequences?

title: Valkyries and Choice: Selection, Honor, and Service
body: Valkyries are associated with selection in battle and the afterlife halls. In a modern study context, you can treat them as symbols of “choice under pressure” and “honor in constraint,” useful for reflection prompts and ethical decision-making exercises.
